paras: The attempted lynching of Solomon Glasgow and Charles Strickland took place at Holly Springs, Marshall County, Mississippi, on the night of April 11, 1903, when a mob came to the jail to hang two Black prisoners who were under sentence of death. Sheriff McWilliams disguised the two men and got them away through the crowd, and the mob found only the sheriff's son, whom it forced to give up the keys. Both men were hanged legally at Holly Springs on June 30, 1903.

Glasgow, described in a wire report as "a negro preacher," had been convicted of killing a young white male near Holly Springs, named in later reports as Neill or Neil Jones. Strickland, by one account, "had murdered another negro"; Jackson reports said he had shot Deputy Sheriff Cal Thompson during an arrest in 1895 or 1896.

Glasgow, Strickland and a third Black prisoner, Dave Logan, were sentenced to hang at Holly Springs on Friday, April 10. On April 9 the governor commuted Logan's sentence to life imprisonment, and Glasgow's appeal to the state supreme court stayed his execution. A Holly Springs dispatch that day reported "some uneasiness" that people from the neighborhood of the killing would take the law into their own hands.

According to a dispatch datelined Mobile, April 12, a mob appeared at the Holly Springs jail on the night of April 11 seeking the two condemned men. Sheriff McWilliams disguised his prisoners and left through the crowd, "the condemned men mingling with the others." The mob forced the keys from the sheriff's son, "rushed upon the boy" when it found the cells empty, and then searched the sheriff's home.

The Sun said the prisoners went to the state penitentiary at Jackson, while a later Jackson report said the sheriff took Glasgow to an adjoining county and then a distant one. No report names a member of the mob, records an injury, or mentions an arrest.

In May the Mississippi supreme court affirmed both death sentences and set the hangings for June 30 at Holly Springs. The Jackson report on the decision recalled that "an attempt was made to lynch him after the arrest" and credited "the shrewdness of Sheriff McWilliams" with saving Glasgow.

Strickland and Glasgow were hanged on June 30, 1903, on the same gallows at Holly Springs before a crowd given as "several thousand" or 3,000. On the scaffold Strickland denied firing the fatal shot, and Glasgow denied his guilt and repudiated a pamphlet sold that day as his confession.

All of the coverage located came from white papers, and the fullest account of the attempt ran in the New York Sun on April 13 under the headlines "Sheriff Outwits a Mob" and "Rioters Wanted a Hanging." The Sun called the prisoners "the two negro murderers held there under sentence," treated Glasgow's guilt as settled, and made the sheriff's ruse the center of the story.

Within days the Port Gibson Reveille and the Brandon News reduced it to one line in a news digest about "a mob of masked men" who tried to lynch "two negroes." Another digest, carried from April 17 to 25 in Kentucky, Mississippi and Arkansas papers, said only that "an unsuccessful attempt was made to lynch two men."

Later Mississippi coverage folded the attempt into accounts of the legal case, praising the sheriff's "shrewdness" and offering the quickly affirmed sentence as "a good illustration of the quickness of Mississippi justice." The Hattiesburg Daily Progress, reporting the hanging, wrote that Glasgow's crime "was wholly without provocation" and that sentiment against him had been "very high in the community." The Sun's brief on the execution said both men "were put to death for the murder of whites" and added that Black people called legal hangings "sky journeys."

The April wire report placed the attempt after Glasgow's conviction, while later Jackson reports said it came "after the arrest" and mentioned one prisoner, though both describe the sheriff passing through the crowd. The reports also disagree on Strickland's victim, whom the April dispatch called "another negro" but whom the more detailed Mississippi accounts named as Deputy Sheriff Cal Thompson.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Solomon Glasgow and Charles Strickland
bases: A mob came to the Holly Springs jail to hang two Black prisoners under death sentence and was thwarted when the sheriff removed them (A3, A5, A11); an attempted lynching.

A mob acting without authority sought to hang two prisoners accused and convicted of murder (A3, A11), but the sheriff got them away and no one was killed (A3, A5); this is an attempted lynching, not a completed one. Both men were later executed legally (A14, A15).

The Mobile wire account (A3), a separate digest item describing 'masked men' (A5), and the later Jackson report on the supreme court decision (A11, A12) independently agree that a mob tried to lynch Glasgow and was foiled by Sheriff McWilliams.

accounts.gist: A mob tried to lynch the two condemned men on the night of April 11; the sheriff disguised them and escaped through the crowd, the mob forced the keys from his son and searched his house, and the prisoners were taken to the penitentiary at Jackson.

framing.detail: The Sun headlined 'Sheriff Outwits a Mob' and 'Rioters Wanted a Hanging', calling the prisoners 'the two negro murderers' and treating the sheriff's escape as the story.
Syndicated digests reduced the episode to a single line among world news, one with 'masked men' and 'negroes', the other naming no race.
Mississippi reports praised the sheriff's 'shrewdness' while citing the quick affirmed death sentence as 'a good illustration of the quickness of Mississippi justice'.

conflicts.note: The contemporary wire and digest accounts say two; the Hattiesburg texts of the later reports focus on Glasgow alone, and the Sea Coast Echo's copy of the same report says 'prisoners'.
